title: Diwali 'Acidity' or Something Serious? Doctors Explain Reflux and Heart Attack Warning Signs
excerpt: Late dinners and rich festive food make heartburn common at Diwali. Mumbai Mirror's doctors explain how reflux differs from cardiac pain, what else 'acidity' can be, and the symptoms that need urgent care.
body:
• Heartburn is usually a burning sensation behind the breastbone, sometimes with a sour taste; cardiac pain is more often pressure, tightness or squeezing that may spread to the arms, back, neck, jaw or stomach.
  • Festive food high in sugar, oil and fat, plus irregular timings and late-night dinners, aggravate acidity, bloating and reflux, doctors told Mumbai Mirror.
  • Smaller portions, an earlier dinner, and waiting at least three hours after eating before lying down are the practical steps doctors and dietitians recommend.
  • Seek urgent care for severe chest or abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss, blood in vomit or black stools — and emergency help for any suspected heart attack.

A late dinner followed by a burning sensation in the chest is a familiar festive-season complaint. Diwali brings elaborate meals, larger portions, alcohol and disrupted eating schedules, and the resulting discomfort is often lumped together as "acidity" — a word that covers everything from occasional heartburn to persistent indigestion, Mumbai Mirror reported. Discomfort after one indulgent meal may pass; symptoms that keep returning deserve closer attention.

First, rule out an emergency

Heartburn and a heart attack can feel alike. Heartburn is usually a burning sensation behind the breastbone, sometimes rising towards the throat with a sour taste. Cardiac pain is more often pressure, tightness or squeezing, and may spread to the arms, back, neck, jaw or stomach, with breathlessness, sweating, nausea or light-headedness. Women in particular may have back or jaw pain, nausea and breathlessness without pronounced chest pain, the report said, citing the American Heart Association's advice to seek emergency help if a heart attack is suspected.

The distinction matters because the two pains overlap. Chest pain from angina, caused by reduced blood supply to the heart, can initially feel similar to heartburn but can occur even without eating and may come with shortness of breath or dizziness, according to Dr Maya Balakrishnan, associate professor of gastroenterology at Baylor College of Medicine, quoted by Drug Today Online. For people with diabetes, high blood pressure or a history of smoking, persistent chest pain should never be ignored. Read the full guidance in Mumbai Mirror's doctor explainer.

What reflux feels like — and what else it could be

Heartburn is the most familiar sign of acid reflux, in which stomach contents flow back into the oesophagus; it can also cause regurgitation, sour burps or an unpleasant taste. Frequent episodes that disrupt daily life may point to gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD), sometimes linked to a hiatus hernia.

"During festivals, we tend to consume foods that are high in sugar, oil and fat, including deep-fried and spicy preparations. These can contribute to acidity, abdominal bloating, cramps and diarrhoea."

— Dr Hozefa Runderawala, consultant gastroenterologist, Saifee Hospital

"Irregular meal timings and late-night dinners can further aggravate these symptoms," said Dr Sujit Nair, consultant in medical gastroenterology at KIMS Hospitals, Thane. Not all "acidity" is reflux, the report noted: indigestion can be linked to functional dyspepsia, gastritis or peptic ulcers, and Helicobacter pylori infection is another common cause of persistent discomfort. Anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate the stomach, and gallstones can cause pain in the upper right abdomen after fatty food.

What to change at the table

Smaller portions, fewer second helpings and an earlier dinner all help. For night-time reflux, the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases recommends waiting at least three hours after eating before lying down, and raising the head of the bed rather than piling up pillows, Mumbai Mirror reported. "Smaller, more frequent meals are preferable to a large quantity of food in one sitting. Eating dinner early is equally important," Dr Runderawala said.

Nutritionist Kajal Bhathena and Richa Anand, head of dietetics at LH Hiranandani Hospital, advised planning around the feast: a fibre- and protein-rich breakfast, a light lunch if dinner will be heavy, sweets and fried food in moderation eaten slowly, and a gentle five-minute walk after meals.

Medication and when to see a doctor

Antacids neutralise acid for short-term relief, alginate preparations form a barrier against reflux, and proton pump inhibitors reduce acid production — but their use and duration should be guided by a doctor, and needing over-the-counter remedies often is itself a reason to get checked, the report said. See a doctor for recurring symptoms, disturbed sleep or difficulty swallowing. "Severe abdominal or chest pain should never automatically be attributed to acidity," Dr Nair said.
